scorecard.behaviourOracle: PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / Lua 5.4 via lupa

families.name: Prometheus
families.summary: Open-source Lua 5.1 / basic Luau obfuscator written in Lua (levno-710).
families.detect: Signatures verified against output of the real tool for every step and preset.
limits: Vmify (the flattened register VM) is unflattened: the dispatcher is walked, every block is turned back into statements and the control flow is rebuilt (also for the two Vmify layers of the Strong preset). The output behaves like the obfuscated script on real Lua 5.1; the original variable and function names are not in the output and cannot be recovered.

The anti-tamper check that Medium and Strong compile into the VM is removed by taint analysis when it is separable from the program; if a script mixes the two it is left alone and the step reports why.
String decoders (EncryptStrings, ConstantArray) are evaluated only when sandboxed evaluation is switched on.
Recovery of the Strong preset takes several seconds in the browser (the two layers are rebuilt one after the other).

families.name: Hercules
families.summary: Open-source Lua obfuscator with a module pipeline (zeusssz).
families.detect: Signatures verified against output of the real tool for every module and preset.

versions.note: last commit whose watermark says v1.5 (2024-11-03): first virtual machine (Compiler/c.lua), StringToExpressions, WrapInFunction, compressor
first commit whose watermark says v1.5 (2024-09-22): text modules only, no virtual machine
last commit whose watermark says v1.6 (2025-01-25): anti_tamper added
last commit whose watermark says v1.6.2 (2026-04-30)
last commit whose watermark says v2.0.0 (2026-06-16): manifest.lua, presets, rewritten compiler (Compiler/*.lua)

limits: The bytecode-encoding module hides a compiled Lua 5.4 chunk behind a hex string and an offset. With sandboxed evaluation on, the chunk is read out, decompiled and put in place of the script; without it the module is only detected. The chunk carries debug information, so the original local and function names come back.

The virtual-machine module (revisions 1.6.2 and later, VMGenerator.lua) is read back without running anything: the program text (base-94 digits over a shuffled alphabet, bytes written as pairs with a backslash) is decoded, the Lua 5.1 chunk in it is decompiled and put where the interpreter was started, and the interpreter’s declarations are dropped. Constants the tool’s serialiser measured with `#` and therefore left out when a nil sits among them are put back only where the instructions leave one possible slot; where they leave more than one the choice is ranked and the report says so, and where constants are really missing from the file the module is refused (sample s06 of the corpus is such a case: the values are not in the output the tool wrote). Names are the decompiler’s: the original ones are not in the data.
The virtual-machine module of revisions 1.5 and 1.6 (Compiler/c.lua, a different interpreter and data format) is detected and flagged; its program is not recovered (10% fidelity, measured).

Function inlining is undone: closures pasted at each call site become one local function again, placed where the hole the tool left for the deleted definition is when the text still has it. Original function names are not recoverable.

The renaming module renames `self` in method bodies without declaring it (a defect of the tool): the renamed global is read as `self` again when every use of it is inside a method that does not use `self`, and the report says that it was inferred.

Revisions 1.5 and 1.6: the coin-flip guard of the control-flow module is removed; the older modules (string encoding, garbage code, opaque predicates, wrappers) share their patterns with later revisions and are measured per revision in the Versions table.
The tool itself produced non-equivalent output for some module/sample pairs (see the "tool broken" column); those cases are excluded from behaviour claims.

families.name: Luraph
families.summary: Commercial virtualising obfuscator for Lua and Luau (lura.ph). Per-script VM; v14 and v15 are current.
families.detect: Banner comments only. No real Luraph output could be obtained here, so structural detection is heuristic.
limits: Luraph generates a different virtual machine for every script. Static recovery of the original source from a v14/v15 VM is not something this tool can do, and no output of the real obfuscator was available to test against.

families.name: MoonSec V3
families.summary: Commercial Roblox-oriented Lua obfuscator with a VM loader.
families.detect: Banner comments only; no real output obtained.
limits: VM-based loader; not recoverable statically.

families.name: MoonVeil
families.summary: Commercial obfuscator (moonveil.cc) with selectable virtualisation, function encryption and control-flow flattening (macros MV_VM, MV_ENC_FUNC, MV_CFF, MV_OMIT). One real output was read (banner "generated using MoonVeil 2.0.25"): functions lifted into a table, flattened bootstrap code, Z85 + XOR strings, bit32 expressions for numbers, and VM-compiled functions stored as one compressed Z85 text (read back from that data by the VM reader when the interpreter has the shape of the script that was studied).
families.detect: Banner by its text (the version in it is what the file claims) and the table-and-permutation shape structurally. Five scripts of four versions were read, none of them stored here: 1.4.5, 2.0.25 (supplied by a user), 2.0.26 and 2.1.0 (two scripts) from public deobfuscator repositories. No MoonVeil output could be generated (the tool is closed and hosted), so there is no scorecard row; per-version records are in data/research/format-records.json and are re-measured by tools/formats/measure.mjs when the scripts are present.
limits: Read back statically: the strings (Z85 text plus an XOR cipher), the numbers (bit32 expressions) and the table of cells, which makes the program’s plain Lua readable. The bootstrap permutation is read in both spellings seen (2.0.25 and 2.0.26/2.1.0, where the flattened bootstrap scrambles the statements), and the cell layout (where the index, the value and the self reference sit) is read from the script, not fixed: it differs between 2.0.25, 2.0.26 and 2.1.0.

Version 2.0.25 only: the function MoonVeil compiled to its own VM is read back too, without running anything (data layout, opcode table and instruction layouts are taken from the script’s own interpreter code).

Versions 2.0.26 and 2.1.0: strings and numbers are decoded (for the one 2.0.26 script with a hand-made reference, 77 of its 81 string literals are in the output, including every URL), but the VM reader does not fit the interpreter of these builds ("the interpreter does not have the expected shape") and the control-flow-flattened functions are not all unflattened (the initial state of the dispatcher is not a constant). The program stays a table of decoded functions; fidelity against the reference is 21%. The confidence is capped for that reason (0.60, medium); it was 0.90 before this was measured.

Version 1.4.5: a different layout (no function table): constants and cells are decoded, three dispatcher loops of 8, 135 and 259 blocks remain, and a 28888-character encoded blob is left. No reference exists, so fidelity is not measured; the confidence is low (0.50).

MV_CFF, MV_ENC_FUNC and MV_VM are the vendor’s documented macros (per-function virtualisation, encryption keyed at run time, control-flow flattening, MV_OMIT to exclude one); MV_ENC_FUNC bodies need their run-time key and are not recovered. The vendor’s documentation site could not be read from this environment, so the macro list is from search results quoting it.

families.name: IronBrew 1
families.summary: The first IronBrew (Lua 5.1 VM obfuscator for Roblox): a header comment "this file was generated using ironbrew1" and one wrapper function with dozens of one- and two-letter parameters. A reconstruction engine for it exists in the dynamic service (api/_engine/luraph); the static pipeline only identifies it.
families.detect: Header comment and the wrapper shape, read on 24 real scripts of a public collection (24 of 24 identified, 12 of them held out when the rule was written). The dynamic service has an IronBrew 1 engine (see the Reconstruct tab); the static pipeline does not rebuild the VM.
documentedTechniques: one wrapper function with duplicated parameter names
untestedTechniques: one wrapper function with duplicated parameter names
limits: Identified, not rebuilt statically: the confidence is capped low (0.27 on three scripts).

families.name: MoonSec V2
families.summary: Older MoonSec generation: a global `Protected_by_MoonSecV2` with a discord invite, then a loader that assigns its VM to the global `_msec`. Read on the scripts of a public collection; no generator was available.
families.detect: The Protected_by_MoonSecV2 banner variable and the _msec assignment, read on the scripts of a public collection. Some files filed under MoonSecV2 there are other tools’ output (a "Protected by Mnx Obfuscator", a "DELTA V3"); they are reported as an unrecognised vendor banner, not as MoonSec.
documentedTechniques: constant arithmetic with # of tables and strings
untestedTechniques: constant arithmetic with # of tables and strings
limits: VM loader: identified, not rebuilt.

families.name: wYnFuscate
families.summary: Obfuscator (wynfuscate.com) whose scripts begin "Protected by wYnFuscate" and one wrapper `return(function(vE,vZ,vu,...)` that rebuilds getfenv from string.char codes. Read on the scripts of a public collection.
families.detect: The "Protected by wYnFuscate" header and the wrapper that rebuilds getfenv from string.char codes, read on 22 scripts of a public collection.
limits: VM: identified, not rebuilt. One recovery run took 7 s on a 245 KB script; no crash on any.

families.name: Boronide
families.summary: Obfuscator whose scripts begin with a "Boronide, vX" comment and run a credit string through :gsub('(.*)', function(d) ...) whose body is a state loop. Read on the scripts of a public collection.
families.detect: The "Boronide[™] [Free|Premium] Obfuscation, vX" header (v0.3.0 to v0.7.0 were found) and the credit string run through :gsub('(.*)', function ...), read on the scripts of a public collection.
limits: Opaque state loops and a VM: identified, not rebuilt.

families.name: RBXLuaObfuscator
families.summary: Small Roblox-targeted obfuscator (kosuke14, no licence, 2022) that does not call loadstring: it embeds a Lua lexer, parser and interpreter written in Lua (a few thousand characters of generated text) and hands it the program as a list of one-character decimal-escape strings, after decoy functions built from arithmetic that cancels.
families.detect: Output of the real tool (kosuke14/RBXLuaObfuscator, run in the isolated Lua state; no licence, so the fixtures are in the git-ignored obfuscated-local/): the program is a list of one-character decimal escapes handed to a Lua compiler the script carries (there is no loadstring). Found by shape: the final call, the table.concat of the list, and a lexer that names Lua’s keywords.
documentedTechniques: embedded Lua compiler instead of loadstring
program as a list of decimal-escape characters
untestedTechniques: embedded Lua compiler instead of loadstring
program as a list of decimal-escape characters
limits: The program text is a plain constant and is read without running anything; the output of the tool is identical in behaviour (8 of 8 samples on PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / 5.4) and 100% in fidelity. The tool does not rename anything, so original names are kept. Only the 2022 revision exists.

families.name: SnowVeil
families.summary: Obfuscator that stamps "This file was generated using SnowVeil v1 [discord invite]". No documentation of the tool itself was found. One public sample was read (as text, never as an authority): a VM in one pcall with a collector, a getter that hands out builtins by library and member name, a custom base-85 container, varint-coded constant pools and environment probes through Roblox objects (Path2D, Vector3, CFrame).
families.detect: Banner ("generated using SnowVeil v1") and, without it, the builtin getter (one local function asked for string / table / math / bit32 / Vector3 / CFrame members by name): 0.97 and 0.75. One public sample was read as text and run in the sandboxed environment; nothing about the tool’s own documentation could be found.
documentedTechniques: checksums that make the script error() when the environment differs
untestedTechniques: checksums that make the script error() when the environment differs
limits: The script is a VM in one pcall with a collector, a custom base-85 container, varint-coded constant pools and checksums that make it call error() when the environment differs. Detected and flagged as not recovered: 35% confidence, measured.

The behaviour trace cannot get past the checks: the script probes Path2D objects (GetPositionOnCurve, GetTangentOnCurve, GetLength, GetBoundingRect, GetControlPoints) and the offline Path2D model has no answer for GetBoundingRect, so the run stops at error() after 93 recorded statements. Making it up would be a guess; the answers need a recording from the real engine (--studio) that was not available.
Only version 1 and one script were seen. Another build or setting is unconfirmed.

families.name: Kirus
families.summary: Obfuscator that stamps "This file was protected by Kirus obfuscator v1.5". No public source or documentation was found. One real output was read: a bytecode VM written in Lua with a custom base-85 blob, runtime-keyed constant pools and encrypted instruction regions.
families.detect: Taken from one real script (supplied by a user and not stored here): the banner comment and the entry call setmetatable({...}, {}):name(bit32, string, table, math, type, error, pcall, getfenv or debug.getfenv, ...). Nothing else was available.
limits: A bytecode VM with a custom base-85 container, a keystream and rotation, opaque-predicate dispatch and runtime-keyed constants. The container was cut into regions and measured, not decoded; the program is not recovered.

The identifiers the VM builds from XOR pairs are decoded by plain arithmetic on literals (loadstring, getgenv, setfenv, getrawmetatable, executor names). That shows what the runtime touches, not what the program does.
The behavioural trace can say what an authorised run of it does, but only when the user switches it on. Nothing was run for this project.

families.name: IronBrew 2
families.summary: Open-source (MIT) Lua 5.1 obfuscator in C# that compiles a script with luac and re-emits it as a custom register VM plus a compressed, XOR-masked program string.
families.detect: The prelude (LZW + XOR deserialiser, wrapper function names) is matched structurally; the opcode handlers are matched by alpha-equivalent form against the handler templates in IronBrew 2's own C# source.
limits: Recovery reads the embedded chunk instead of running the VM: handlers are identified by shape, operand transforms are solved symbolically, the Lua 5.1 chunk is rebuilt and decompiled. A handler that matches no template stops the recovery with an error instead of guessing.
Local variable names, comments and the original function layout are not in the bytecode, so they are not recoverable (names are regenerated; some local functions come back as expressions).

The "strings" option decrypts every literal with a routine written out in place. Recovery finds those stretches (only constants, only pure standard functions, no closures) and replaces each by the text it computes, using the sandbox interpreter on that stretch alone; it needs no consent because nothing but the stretch is run. Other register-reuse noise remains, so the result is partial.

The "flow" option of the real tool produced output that does not run correctly on its own for five of eight samples (see the "tool broken" column); recovery there is judged against the original program, not against the broken output.
Only IronBrew 2 as built from the public MIT source is covered. Forks that change the VM template or the serialiser need their own templates.

families.name: LuaObfuscator.com
families.summary: Web obfuscation service (luaobfuscator.com) with several protection levels. Its free tier writes an ASCII-art header ending "LuaObfuscator.com (Alpha x.y.z) ~ Much Love, Ferib", read on the scripts of a public collection; a script without the header is only a signature at this point.
families.detect: Generic string-escape and constant-table heuristics only.
limits: No real output obtained to test against.

families.name: 77fuscator
families.summary: Obfuscator seen only through its "77fuscator <version>" banner; no documentation was found.
families.detect: Banner string only.
limits: Structure unknown.

families.name: PSU
families.summary: Commercial obfuscator (psu.dev). Every script of the public collection (versions 4.0.A and 4.5.A) keeps the string "This file was obfuscated using PSU Obfuscator <version>" as a local of its wrapper `return(function(e, ...)` and reads its constants from a table with numeric and short-string keys. Only identified here.
families.detect: No signature known.
documentedTechniques: wrapper function with a constant table
untestedTechniques: wrapper function with a constant table
limits: Nothing public to verify against.

families.name: Loadstring packers
families.summary: A class of packers, not one tool: the program is encoded and handed to loadstring. The examples were written for this project from the documented encodings; they are not the output of any real obfuscator.
families.detect: Not a single signature: the loadstring-layer trait is reported. Recovery is measured on packers written for this project (tests/corpus/tools/gen_loaders.mjs), not on any real tool.
limits: Literal, folded and string.char payloads are unwrapped without running anything. A payload computed by a decoder (hex, base64, XOR, URL escapes, ...) is read only when sandboxed evaluation is on, and only when the script is nothing but that loader: the other statements may use standard libraries and local variables, nothing else.
A script that does anything else around the loader (touches the game, writes globals, prints) is never replaced wholesale; Dump still shows the text it loads.
Payloads that read `...`, return values, or need the network (`HttpGet`) are left alone. Compiled Lua 5.1 and 5.4 payloads are decompiled.

These are generic packers I wrote from the encodings other tools document. Whether a real obfuscator that uses the same encodings is handled depends on its decoder staying within the standard libraries; none of them was run.

families.name: Colisseum
families.summary: Open-source (AGPL-3.0) Lua / Luau obfuscator written in Lua (de-TourLLC). Presets easy, medium, hard and full are source-level; total and fortress compile the program for a VM.
families.detect: Signatures verified against output of the real tool for every preset: the credit line, the error brand, the coli_ names, the tamper guard block and the VM entry call. The AGPL-3.0 licence of the tool does not allow committing its output, so the fixtures are generated locally (tests/corpus/tools/gen_external.py, run through the isolated runner) and the tests that use them skip when they are absent.
documentedTechniques: tamper guard (debug hook, executor globals, replaced standard functions, line-number check)
untestedTechniques: tamper guard (debug hook, executor globals, replaced standard functions, line-number check)
limits: easy, medium, hard and full are source-level: the tamper guard is recognised by its strings and removed without being run, the string decryptor is evaluated in the sandbox, and the junk branches are dropped. The output prints what the original program prints; names are guesses from use.

The decryptor multiplies past 2^53 and was written for Lua 5.4 integers (it gives noise on Lua 5.1, LuaJIT and Luau doubles). The sandbox therefore evaluates it both ways and keeps the reading that is text; if neither is, the strings are left encoded and the report says so. Without the sandbox the strings stay encoded.

total (native VM) and fortress (register VM with an encrypted bytecode blob) are detected from the VM entry call and flagged as not recovered: the program exists only as data for an interpreter. Recovery is not attempted.

The behavioural trace is stopped by the tamper guard of every preset except easy, because the trace’s stand-in environment defines executor functions and the guard counts them (error 0x6B0C). Remove the guard first (medium, hard, full: Deobfuscate, then Trace the result). In the plain sandbox total runs to the end and fortress stops at 0x3E44 (the guard sees the sandbox’s debug library is not native).
The total and fortress fixtures only run without an instruction-count hook, on LuaJIT: their anti-tamper treats a hook as an attack, so they were verified with tests/corpus/tools/run_lua_nohook.py.

families.name: Zenfus
families.summary: Open-source (MIT) obfuscator based on IronBrew 2 (Zaenalos): the script is compiled with luac 5.4 and run by a generated VM.
families.detect: Signatures from the tool’s source and verified on its output: the wrapper (function(pack, move, unpack, env, pCall, Err) ...) and the VM names lua_wrap_state, run_vm and hexToString.
limits: The program is compiled with luac 5.4, its constants are encrypted, dead instructions and super-operators are added, and a generated VM runs the hex-encoded stream. It is detected and flagged as not recovered; no lifter for its instruction format was written.

The behavioural trace works (the sandbox gained Lua 5.4 bitwise operators, goto, string.unpack, _ENV and integer arithmetic for it) and reproduces what the original program does for every fixture where the tool’s own output is correct. A trace describes one run; it is not the original source.
Zenfus’s own output misbehaves for six of the eight programs (see the "tool broken" column); those fixtures are excluded from behaviour claims.

families.name: Simple-Lua-Obfuscator
families.summary: Small obfuscator (CloudHub111, no licence file): the script is written as codes, base64-encoded, cut into five-character pieces and loaded at run time.
families.detect: The fixed helper names of the tool’s template (_0x38ndf, _0x93mdw, _0x47fjs, _0x62tdg, _0x29dke). The repository has no licence file, so the fixtures are generated locally and not committed.
limits: The program is written as decimal escapes, base64-encoded, cut into five-character pieces and loaded at run time. With the sandbox on, the loader is run alone to read the text it hands to load, and that text replaces the script. Without the sandbox the layer is only detected.

This is a loader-style packer: anything the loader does besides decoding (touching other globals, printing) stops the replacement. Variable names of the original are kept because the payload is the original source.

families.name: AztupBrew
families.summary: A fork of IronBrew 2 ("AztupBrew(Fork of IronBrew2): obfuscation; Version 2.7.2" in its output). Only one public sample was found; its VM data layout differs from IronBrew 2, so the IronBrew 2 rebuild does not apply.
families.detect: The banner (AztupBrew(Fork of IronBrew2): obfuscation; Version 2.7.2) and the eight-local prelude of the VM. One public sample exists (a script that prints "1", in a repository without a licence), so structure was checked against it only.
limits: A fork of IronBrew 2 whose VM data layout differs from the one the IronBrew 2 rebuild reads. The rebuild is not attempted on it; a VM is reported as not recovered.
The trace of the one sample reproduces its output. With one sample, nothing is known about how other settings of the tool look.

families.detect: Name mention only.
limits: The repository is a README with screenshots: no code and no sample output. Nothing to verify against.

families.summary: Hosted Roblox obfuscator (zerolua.pages.dev). Its GitHub repository holds only a README; no code and no sample output.
families.detect: Name mention only.
limits: The repository is a README: no code and no sample output. The service is hosted; its output was not available.

families.summary: Paid service advertised through a Discord invite. Its GitHub repository holds a README and a file containing the invite: no code and no sample output.
families.detect: Name mention only.
limits: The repository is an advertisement for a paid service: a README and a file holding a Discord invite.

families.name: NeuroForge VM
families.summary: The name used by the repository "Lua-Polymorph-VM-Forge". It contains no Lua code: a marketing README, images, and an obfuscated web page with a download button. Treat it as untrusted; nothing in it was run.
families.detect: Name mention only.
limits: The repository (Lua-Polymorph-VM-Forge) contains no Lua: a README, images, an hourly workflow that rewrites a stamp file, and an obfuscated web page with a download button. It was read as text only and nothing from it was run. Treat it as untrusted.

families.name: Stealth-X
families.summary: Hosted obfuscator for Lua 5.1 and Luau (Roblox) with a Beautify, Minify, Weak (no VM) and four VM presets. Its output starts with an ASCII-art header reading "This file secured by StealthxProtect Gen3.2". Only the five sample outputs in its public repository were read; the repository has no licence and no source.
families.detect: Taken from the five sample outputs in the tool’s public repository (one 11-line program at the Weak, Performance, Standard, Strong and Maximum presets), read as text and never run: the StealthxProtect header, the "STX@" program string and the handler table keyed by 32-bit numbers. The repository has no licence, so none of it is stored here.
limits: The four VM presets are detected and flagged as not recovered. Before this signature existed they were rated as plain minified code at 90% confidence, which was wrong.
The Weak preset has a constant array with swaps and a string cipher; its structure also matches the Prometheus rules (80%). Which of the two it resembles is not decided here.
Only one program was seen at each preset, so how the tool treats other code is unknown. The hosted tool was not used.

families.name: AzureVM
families.summary: Open-source (MIT) Lua 5.1 VM obfuscator by LionHub-Pino, built on Prometheus. Reads Lua 5.1 bytecode and emits an interpreter with an encoded payload: seeded opcode map, rolling instruction encoding, per-prototype field layouts. Preset names with "Luraph" in them are its own labels (its README says it is not Luraph); its payload is tagged "LPH" like Luraph’s.
families.detect: Signatures from the tool’s source (MIT) and verified on its output: the header comment (-- Generated by AzureVM (template mode N)), the 12-library prelude, the __az_retry_ locals and the [=[LPH payload tag. The Balanced preset writes a Prometheus-style script and is recognised by the existing Prometheus rules plus the -- AzureXPino watermark.
limits: The program is compiled to Lua 5.1 bytecode, its instructions are encoded with a seeded opcode map and a rolling cipher, and a generated interpreter runs it. The VM is detected and flagged as not recovered; no lifter for this format was written.
The Balanced preset is not a VM: its Prometheus-style transforms are partly reverted by the existing passes.

Presets named after Luraph are the tool’s own labels; its README says it is not Luraph. The payload tag LPH is the same three letters Luraph uses, which is a naming overlap, not evidence of shared code.
Fixtures were generated here by running the tool inside the isolated harness; its outputs are committed because the licence is MIT.

families.name: Simple Open source Lua Obfuscator (page)
families.summary: A single HTML page (iamsopotatoe, MIT) that strips comments, renames locals with regular expressions, encodes strings for a _D decoder, writes numbers as sums, and adds junk statements and always-true wrappers. Its author says it gives no meaningful protection and may break code.
families.detect: The _D decoder line the page writes in front of every script, and its (_D({codes})) call sites. Fixtures were made by running the page’s own JavaScript unchanged under Node with no network and no file access beyond the output folder.
documentedTechniques: string codes with a key decoder
limits: The page renames locals by regular expression (so it can break code that its author did not test) and writes strings as number lists for the _D decoder. The decoder is a subtraction with wrap-around, recognised only in the exact form the page writes it and computed on the literal lists, so no sandbox is needed.
Three of the eight outputs of the page itself do not behave like their originals (its regular-expression renaming breaks some programs), so behaviour is only compared for the other five.
The author says in the page itself that it gives no meaningful protection. The numbers here measure how much of the original is recovered, not how strong the tool is.

families.name: Clyde
families.summary: Open-source (MIT) Luau obfuscator written in TypeScript (sfr-development), also sold as a hosted service ("Clyde V3"): AST passes, then optional stack-VM output with an ASCII-art header. Its README warns of rebrands by others.
families.detect: The ASCII-art header of the VM modes (the site name and a build id), string.char fetched as ("")["\99\104\97\114"], and the XOR string decoder with an always-true cache test. The rename-only mode leaves no marker, so it is not recognised by name.
limits: The rename and string/flow modes are reverted statically. The VM modes (vm, vm-max) hide the program behind a stack or register VM and are detected and flagged as not recovered.

The repository’s README warns of rebrands and sellers using the name. The header seen in output is the hosted service’s, so a script with it may come from the service rather than from the open-source build; this is not a finding about who made a script.
vm-max (LZSS plus a cipher layer) could not be run on the reference interpreters here, so its behaviour was not compared.
